entry.title: [law] Supreme Court grants cert in Crowther v. Board of Regents to resolve whether employees can sue for sex discrimination under Title IX
entry.summary: The Supreme Court agreed to hear Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia to decide whether employees — not just students — can bring sex discrimination suits under Title IX, a question that has divided the lower courts and could significantly expand or contract workplace discrimination protections in educational institutions.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court agreed to hear Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia to decide whether employees — not just students — can bring sex discrimination suits under Title IX, a question that has divided the lower courts and could significantly expand or contract workplace discrimination protections in educational institutions.

Title IX, enacted in 1972, prohibits sex discrimination in education programs or activities receiving federal financial assistance. While the statute's primary application has historically been to student discrimination — including sexual harassment, athletic program equity, and admissions — lower courts have split on whether employees of covered institutions can also invoke Title IX as a basis for discrimination suits, in addition to or instead of relying on Title VII, the general employment discrimination statute. The case comes to the Court from Georgia, where Crowther, a university employee, brought suit under Title IX rather than Title VII. The specific procedural and substantive differences between the two statutes — including statute of limitations, administrative exhaustion requirements, and available remedies — make the choice of statutory vehicle legally significant rather than merely tactical. The Court added the case to its 2026–27 oral argument calendar on May 19, 2026.

Why it matters: If the Court holds that Title IX covers employees, it would substantially expand the pool of potential plaintiffs in sex discrimination suits against educational institutions, since schools and universities employ large numbers of faculty, staff, and administrators who would gain an additional statutory avenue for discrimination claims. Title IX and Title VII differ in meaningful procedural ways: Title VII requires exhaustion of EEOC administrative remedies before suit, while Title IX does not; this makes Title IX potentially a faster and less bureaucratically burdened path to federal court for employment discrimination claims. Conversely, a ruling that Title IX does not cover employees would concentrate all workplace discrimination claims in educational settings under Title VII — potentially a result that some institutions and their insurers would prefer for its procedural predictability. The Roberts Court has shown a willingness to constrain implied rights of action and narrow statutory scope in recent years, and Crowther will test whether that narrowing tendency extends to a statute — Title IX — that has been a broadly understood anti-discrimination cornerstone since the 1970s. For plaintiff attorneys in employment discrimination, the case may determine whether Title IX remains a viable alternative theory in cases involving school and university employees or becomes limited to student-facing discrimination exclusively.

entry.title: [law] Supreme Court refuses to reinstate Virginia's Democratic-drawn redistricting map, letting Republican-drawn districts stand for upcoming elections
entry.summary: The Supreme Court declined an emergency request to reinstate Virginia's Democratic-drawn congressional map, leaving Republican-drawn districts in place for upcoming elections after a state court found the Democratic map improperly favored one party.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court declined an emergency request to reinstate Virginia's Democratic-drawn congressional map, leaving Republican-drawn districts in place for upcoming elections after a state court found the Democratic map improperly favored one party.

Virginia's redistricting saga involves competing maps drawn by Democratic and Republican commissioners following the 2020 census, adjudicated by the Virginia Supreme Court. The Democratic-drawn map was struck down by a Virginia court on grounds that it constituted partisan gerrymandering under Virginia's own state constitutional standards — a distinct basis from federal law. The Republican-drawn map was reinstated as the default. Applicants sought an emergency stay from the U.S. Supreme Court to reinstate the Democratic map, arguing the process that produced the Republican map was also procedurally flawed. The Court declined without noted dissent, allowing the Republican-drawn map to govern upcoming elections. The Virginia case is notable because it involves state constitutional anti-gerrymandering standards rather than federal law — a ground the U.S. Supreme Court has said it cannot police (Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019) — making the Virginia court's application of its own state constitution the primary legal lever in play.

Why it matters: The Virginia decision is a reminder that post-Rucho redistricting litigation has shifted largely to state courts applying state constitutional standards, with the U.S. Supreme Court playing a more limited emergency-stay role rather than a substantive review function. The refusal to reinstate the Democratic map means the congressional delegation from Virginia — a competitive state — will be elected from Republican-drawn districts for at least the next election cycle, with potentially significant effects on the partisan composition of the U.S. House. For redistricting practitioners, the case illustrates the double-edged nature of state anti-gerrymandering provisions: they can cut against either party's preferred maps, and courts applying them may invalidate maps drawn by either side without a clear constitutional resolution about what a neutral map requires. The U.S. Supreme Court's consistent reluctance to intervene in partisan gerrymandering disputes — even via emergency stays — leaves redistricting as an area where federal constitutional law provides minimal protection and the outcomes depend almost entirely on which party controls the state legislature, redistricting commission, or state judiciary at the relevant moment.

entry.title: [law] Judge rules 3D-printed ghost gun and manifesto admissible in Luigi Mangione murder trial, rejecting defense's prejudice arguments
entry.summary: A New York judge ruled that a 3D-printed untraceable ghost gun recovered near Luigi Mangione's arrest site and a manifesto found on his person are admissible evidence in his murder trial for the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, rejecting defense arguments that the items are more prejudicial than probative.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A New York judge ruled that a 3D-printed untraceable ghost gun recovered near Luigi Mangione's arrest site and a manifesto found on his person are admissible evidence in his murder trial for the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, rejecting defense arguments that the items are more prejudicial than probative.

Luigi Mangione faces murder charges in New York for the December 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Midtown Manhattan. At the time of his arrest in Pennsylvania, law enforcement recovered a 3D-printed ghost gun — an untraceable firearm manufactured without a serial number, which cannot be linked through traditional ATF tracing — and a handwritten manifesto expressing grievances against the health insurance industry. The defense moved to exclude both items, arguing that the ghost gun's association with criminal connotations and the manifesto's inflammatory rhetoric would unfairly prejudice the jury against Mangione before the prosecution established the elements of the crime. The judge rejected both arguments, finding the ghost gun is probative of planning and intent — a weapon specifically designed to avoid tracing evidence connects to deliberate premeditation — and the manifesto provides direct evidence of motive, which is independently admissible as state of mind evidence under New York evidentiary rules.

Why it matters: The admissibility ruling is significant for trial strategy: the ghost gun and manifesto together form the prosecution's most direct evidence of premeditation and motive, the two elements that distinguish first-degree murder from lesser charges. If convicted of first-degree murder in New York, Mangione faces life imprisonment without parole; the manifesto's admission means the jury will hear Mangione's own words connecting his act to a political grievance, which the prosecution will use to establish that the shooting was calculated rather than impulsive. For the defense, the ruling narrows the viable trial strategies substantially — arguing against the weight of both physical evidence and the defendant's own written expression of intent is difficult. The case has drawn extraordinary public attention, with significant polarization in public discourse about the health insurance industry, creating a jury-selection challenge that the court will need to manage carefully. The ghost gun angle also has policy implications: the case has become a prominent example cited in legislative debates over ghost gun regulation, and the trial's outcome may influence state-level legislative momentum on untraceable firearm restrictions in New York and other states.

entry.title: [cybersecurity] Grafana Labs refuses to pay ransom after CoinbaseCarter gang steals source code, betting that transparency outweighs negotiation
entry.summary: Grafana Labs publicly disclosed a ransomware incident in which the CoinbaseCarter threat actor stole source code and demanded payment, then chose to refuse payment and publish a detailed incident report — a transparency-first response that contrasts with the industry norm of quiet settlement.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Grafana Labs publicly disclosed a ransomware incident in which the CoinbaseCarter threat actor stole source code and demanded payment, then chose to refuse payment and publish a detailed incident report — a transparency-first response that contrasts with the industry norm of quiet settlement.

The CoinbaseCarter threat actor — named for its social engineering tactics that impersonate Coinbase support personnel — gained access to Grafana Labs' internal systems and exfiltrated source code before issuing a ransom demand. Grafana Labs made the decision to refuse payment and instead published a comprehensive incident report detailing the attack vector, the extent of the data taken, the company's response, and the technical controls that failed. The decision to go public rather than negotiate quietly is unusual in enterprise software: most companies that experience source code theft opt for confidential settlements or quiet remediation to avoid customer alarm, regulatory scrutiny, and competitive disadvantage from exposing code architecture. Grafana Labs argued that its transparency approach better serves customers — who can make informed security decisions about their deployments — and that paying ransoms funds the criminal ecosystem that creates future attacks. The source code stolen relates to Grafana's observability platform, which is widely deployed in enterprise infrastructure monitoring environments.

Why it matters: Grafana Labs' public refusal is a significant data point in the ongoing debate about ransom payment norms in enterprise cybersecurity. Every paid ransom funds additional criminal operations and signals to threat actors that a given sector is a viable target; every refused ransom marginally increases the operational cost-to-return ratio for ransomware groups. The CoinbaseCarter group's focus on social engineering rather than technical exploitation reflects an industry-wide shift: as technical defenses have improved, the most effective attack vector for credential theft has become human manipulation rather than software vulnerability. For Grafana customers, the stolen source code creates a specific risk calculus: sophisticated adversaries with access to proprietary source code can identify undisclosed vulnerabilities more efficiently than external researchers, creating a window during which Grafana needs to audit and patch any issues before they are exploited. The transparency report approach also has regulatory implications — as mandatory breach disclosure requirements expand under SEC rules and state consumer protection laws, companies that proactively disclose may receive more favorable regulatory treatment than those who disclose only when required.
